a pintle injector has 96–99% combustion efficiency and 35:1 maximum
thrust control range, showing the possibility of thrust control without
significant performance degradation [9]. Based on the successes of the
US lunar landing module engine (LMDE), SpaceX (Falcon 9) Merlin, and
China’s Chang’E 3, which used pintle injectors, several advantages of
pintle injectors, such as thrust control, combustion stability, and easy
scalability, have been verified [4,9,11]. Thus, studies on pintle injectors
are being conducted actively at several universities and research in­
stitutes globally.

Combustion tests based on the total momentum ratio ( _TMR_ ) (0.75,
1.45) changes of fuel-centered single-row discontinuous pintle injectors
(with blockage factor; _BF_ of 0.6/0.3) were conducted at Penn State
University, and relatively high combustion efficiency was confirmed at a
_BF_ of 0.6 and _TMR_ of 1.45 [12]. Researchers at Purdue University
studied combustion performance based on changes in the _TMR_ and
characteristic chamber length (L*) for fuel-centered hole-injection-type
pintle injectors [13]. National University of Defense Technology(NUDT)
of China has reported on the theory and analysis of the injection angle
after propellant collision in the first-row continuous or discontinuous
pintle injector as well as heat load reduction in the recirculation region
based on changes to the row spacing in the two-row configuration

[14–16]. Researchers at Tokyo University in Japan observed the internal
flow field of the ethanol/liquid oxygen (LOx) pintle injector using CH
chemiluminescence and studied the effects of combustion chamber
perturbations as well as changes in the combustion characteristic ve­
locity based on the _TMR_ [17–20]. Investigators at Chungnam National
University in Korea studied the combustion characteristic velocity of the
kerosene pintle injector based on the pintle orifice shape, _TMR_, and

combustion characteristic chamber length [21–25]. Scientists at the
Korea Aerospace University studied the analysis and cold flow test of the
gas–liquid continuous pintle injector based on the opening degree and

_TMR_, recirculation area control method by changes to the injector
shape, pintle orifice shapes, as well as injector and combustion chamber
designs [26–30]. Researchers at Seoul National University studied the
spray characteristics of pintle injectors based on the annulus orifice area
and movable pintles using methane and LOx [31,32].

Although many studies have been conducted on pintle injectors, the
types of propellants, pintle shapes, and annulus combinations used were
diverse; therefore, studies on performance optimizations, such as pro­
pellant mixing efficiency and atomization, are relatively insufficient.
Moreover, research on combustion tests under high-pressure/high-flowrate conditions are sparse. In particular, the tip of the pintle injector is
extremely vulnerable to thermal damage owing to the recirculation area
of high mixing ratio and high heat flux. In previous studies, such thermal
damage was prevented by changing the pintle tip shape, cooling,
coating, and material change. Mulelle, the designer of Merlin engines,
drilled a hole at the pintle tip to allow flow of propellant and achieve
cooling [33]. In TRW, the pintles were made from nickel copper alloys
and coated with TBC (Thermal barrier coating) to increase the thermal
durability of the pintle tip [2]. Researchers at Northrop Grumman
changed the shape and orifice of the pintle injector to prevent thermal
damage of the pintle tip [2]. Chang et al. conducted a study on the
characteristics of the pintle injector and heat transfer based on skip
distance and changes in the pintle 1/2 row distance [16]. Most of these
previous studies on prevention of pintle tip thermal damage have
limited applicability or only showed numerical analyses and
low-pressure combustion tests. Supercritical combustion, which is the
operating area of a high-performance liquid rocket engine, has different
combustion characteristics from subcritical conditions. Therefore, it is
necessary to study the combustion characteristics of liquid-liquid pintle
injectors in supercritical condition.

The present study addresses the 1) design and manufacture of a 1.5tonf class liquid–liquid pintle injector with two-row rectangular orifice
using kerosene and LOx as propellants, 2) results of combustion tests
under supercritical conditions, 3) design change of the pintle injector
and thermal fluid analysis, and 4) verification through a hot firing test.

**2.** **Design and manufacture of the pintle injector**

_2.1._ _Basic design of the pintle injector_

pellant and a surrounding annulus ring. The pintle part supplied with the

central propellant is divided into continuous and discontinuous types in
accordance with the orifice shape, and the propellant sprayed from the
annulus ring collides with that in the pintle orifice and mixes to form a
cone-shaped droplet film. Fig. 1 shows a pintle injector with two rect­
angular rows and discontinuous orifices. The _TMR_, _BF_, diameter ratio
( _DR_ ), skip ratio ( _SR_ ), and orifice shape are the main design factors of the
pintle injector. The _TMR_, which is defined as the ratio of momenta of the
pintle to annulus orifices, and the _BF_, which is defined as the total
circumferential length of the pintle orifice divided by that of the pintle,
are the most important factors in the design of the pintle injector. These
are closely related to the mixing efficiency, shape, and arrangement of
the orifice [12]. The definitions of main design factors are shown in
Table 1.

_2.2._ _Pintle injector design_

From the results of previous studies, it is known that the discontin­
uous two-row pintle injector is more efficient than the continuous singlerow pintle injector and that the second-row flow rate shows maximum
performance at a flow rate ratio of about 15% [34]. In addition, the
propellant inside the pintle injector generally uses an oxidizer for high
thrust, and the fuel injected into the circumference creates a low mixing

ratio recirculation area on the combustion chamber head surface, which
is advantageous for cooling [35]. The _TMR_ and _BF_ show optimal per­
formances as they are closer to 1 in the experimental results of the
previously reported studies [12,25].

For the design of the pintle injector used in this study, the pressure
drop is determined on the basis of the propellant flow rate and injection
area with reference to the results of previous research. Moreover, _DR_ is
set to the recommended value of 3–5 [12]. Finally, using kerosene and
liquid oxygen (central propellant), a 1.5-tonf class liquid–liquid pintle
injector with rectangular two-row orifice, 18 mm diameter, and _BF_ of
86% was designed. The final pintle injector specifications are shown in
Table 2.

The pintle injector and annulus ring were designed separately to
allow testing of various combinations. The propellant supply pipes are
1 <sup>′′</sup> for the pintle injector and 3/4 <sup>′′</sup> for the annulus ring. A temperature
sensor, static pressure sensor, and high-frequency pressure sensor were
installed in each manifold for data acquisition. The assembly shape of
the manufactured pintle head part is as shown in Fig. 2.

_2.3._ _Combustion chamber design_

In general, there are many cooling methods for liquid rocket engines,
such as the ablation, penetration, regenerative, and film cooling
methods as well as thermal barrier coating method (TBC); one or more of
these methods are often applied in the design and fabrication [36]. The
channel-type regenerative and film cooling methods were applied to the
combustion chamber used in this study to meet the cooling performance
under supercritical conditions. In addition, the TBC was applied to the
combustion chamber to increase the thermal stability. The insert-type
film cooling ring assembled between the cylinder and head parts was
designed such that the supplied cooling fluid achieves axial momentum
while circling within the combustion chamber to improve its cooling
performance. To enhance the flexibility of the tests, the cylinder and
nozzle parts were designed separately, where the inner liner was made
of copper alloy and outer jacket was made of stainless steel. These parts
were then assembled using brazing techniques. The combustion cham­
ber design pressure was 7.0 MPa, and a straight-type cooling channel
was designed for convenience for manufacturing. The characteristic
length **_L_** <sup>*</sup> is defined as the ratio of the chamber volume to nozzle throat
area, which is used to specify the propellent stay time in the combustion
chamber. The combustion characteristic length used in this study is
1539.4 mm.

**3.** **Preliminary hot firing test**

_3.1._ _Test facility_

The combustion tests were conducted in a horizontal pressure-fed
ground combustion test facility located at the Korea Aerospace
Research Institute, using kerosene and liquid oxygen as the propellants

[37]. The propellant and cooling water for the combustion test were
filled in each run tank, pressurized to a high value using gaseous ni­
trogen, and supplied to the thrust chamber. The propellant flow rate
supplied to the thrust chamber was measured using a mass flow meter
(oxidant) and turbine flow meter (fuel, cooling water) installed between
the run tank and propellant supply valve, and the propellant supplied to
the thrust chamber was ignited using a methane torch. The electronic
solenoid valve was controlled by an industrial PLC to maintain constant
pressure of the propellant run tank during the hot firing test.

_3.2._ _Configuration of the pintle injector for the test_

combustion chamber parts. The head consists of a pintle injector and
annulus ring, and the combustion chamber consists of a film cooling
